questions.stem: After eating a large carbohydrate-rich meal, a person's blood glucose level rises. Which sequence of events correctly describes the body's response?

options.text: Pancreas detects high glucose → alpha cells release glucagon → liver converts glycogen to glucose
Pancreas detects high glucose → beta cells release insulin → liver converts glucose to glycogen → blood glucose falls
Liver detects high glucose → releases insulin → muscles absorb glycogen
Brain detects high glucose → sends nerve impulses to liver → liver excretes glucose in bile

questions.explanation: When blood glucose rises, beta cells in the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas detect this and release insulin. Insulin causes liver and muscle cells to take up glucose and convert it to glycogen for storage, bringing blood glucose back down to normal.

questions.stem: A person has been exercising for 2 hours without eating. Their blood glucose level drops. How does the body respond to raise blood glucose back to normal?

options.text: The pancreas releases more insulin to break down glycogen
The adrenal glands release adrenaline to slow down metabolism
Alpha cells in the pancreas release glucagon, which stimulates the liver to convert glycogen to glucose
The kidneys filter less glucose from the blood to retain it

questions.explanation: When blood glucose is low, alpha cells in the pancreas release glucagon. Glucagon acts on the liver, stimulating the conversion of stored glycogen back into glucose (glycogenolysis), which is released into the blood to raise glucose levels back to normal.

questions.stem: A student creates a graph showing blood glucose levels after eating. The glucose rises, peaks at 30 minutes, then returns to normal by 2 hours. This return to normal is an example of which type of feedback?

options.text: Positive feedback — the rise in glucose triggers further increases
Negative feedback — the rise in glucose triggers insulin release, which brings glucose back down
No feedback — glucose naturally decreases over time
Positive feedback — insulin amplifies the glucose increase

questions.explanation: This is negative feedback: the deviation from normal (raised glucose) triggers a response (insulin release) that counteracts the change, returning blood glucose to its set point. The response opposes the stimulus, which is the defining feature of negative feedback.

questions.stem: Glycogen is stored in the liver and muscles. Why can only liver glycogen contribute to raising blood glucose levels, not muscle glycogen?

options.text: Muscle cells do not contain glycogen
Muscle cells lack the enzyme needed to release glucose into the blood; they use their glycogen for their own respiration
Muscle glycogen is a different molecule that cannot become glucose
Muscles release glucose into the blood faster than the liver

questions.explanation: Muscle cells lack the enzyme glucose-6-phosphatase, which is needed to convert glucose-6-phosphate into free glucose for release into the blood. Muscle glycogen can only be broken down and used locally by the muscle cells for their own energy needs.

questions.stem: A person with a glucagon-secreting tumour has chronically elevated glucagon levels. What effect would this have on their blood glucose and glycogen stores?

options.text: Blood glucose would be persistently low; glycogen stores would increase
Blood glucose would be persistently high; liver glycogen stores would be depleted
Blood glucose would be normal; glycogen would be unaffected
Blood glucose would fluctuate wildly with no pattern

questions.explanation: Excess glucagon would continuously stimulate the liver to break down glycogen into glucose and release it into the blood. This would cause persistently high blood glucose (hyperglycaemia) and gradual depletion of liver glycogen stores.
